newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS -- Newmont Mining, Santa Fe.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS -- Newmont Mining, Santa Fe.

text.p: A $65 million break-up charge contained in Santa Fe Pacific Gold Corp's merger deal with Homestake Mining Co threatens a key element of Newmont Mining Corp's hostile bid for Santa Fe, the money saving pooling-of-interest accounting.
But despite the accounting hurdle, and Newmont conditioning the deal on it receiving 90 percent of Santa Fe shares, anaylsts said they believe Newmont's bid is superior to that of Homestake.

"More and more people are coming to the conclusion that the accounting will not be an issue. Newmont said they can get a ruling from the SEC before the (Homestake-Santa Fe) shareholder vote, so they will know ahead of time," said Victor Lazarovici, Smith Barney's gold company analyst.
On December 5, Newmont made an unsolicted merger proposal, whereby each Santa Fa shares would be swapped for 0.33 Newmont shares.
Newmont shares closed that day up 3/8 at 47-1/8, a level that valued Santa Fe at $15.55 per share, or $2 billion. Santa Fe Pacific finished December 5 at 14-7/8, up three.

Because the break-up fee is so high, even if Newmont is successful in acquiring Santa Fe, payment of the charge to Homestake may be interpreted as disposition of a substantial corporate asset, analysts said.

Such a dispostion made in the course of a merger or acquisition precludes use of pooling-of-interest, which is preferred over purchase accounting becuase it avoids often huge charges, most often from goodwill.

Four days later, Santa Fe Pacific announced a friendly merger with Homestake Mining at a rate of 1.115 Homestake shares for each Santa Fe share. Terms of the deal then valued Santa Fe at $17.42 per share, or $2.3 billion.

Today, Newmont raised its bid to 0.4 of its shares for each Santa Fe share, equal to $16.10 based on Newmont's 40-1/4 close Tuesday, off 1-1/4, and said it will commence a tender offer if Santa Fe did not call off the Homestake deal and come to the bargaining table.
"This thing could go right to end, with proxies being filed right down to the wire," he said.

Newmont's U.S. Securities and Exchange filing detailing Tuesday's sweetened, and more hostile, offer for Santa Fe states it is "seeking formal interpretive advice" from the SEC concerning the ability of Newmont Mining to account for the offer and and the ... merger as a pooling of interests."

As for the high level of shares required for the deal to be consummated, Lazarovici said, "The good news is that Santa Fe shares were issued just over two years ago as a spin out from Santa Fe Pacific Railroad. The vintage of the paper is fresh so people should be able to get their hands on the stock and deliver it if they so choose."
So the 90 percent level "...should be an issue but not a showstopper," Lazarovici said.
"But Newmont is the better offer, both in terms of current market value and long-term potential," he said.

"Homestake is stuck between a rock and a hard place. They need to do something to develop growth and profitabilty, which takes years to develop internally. They need to fill in the gap with an acquisition," he said.
Over the last year, Homestake Mining shares have declined almost 22 percent, to close at 13-3/4 Tuesday, up 5/8.
Meanwile, Newmont shares have fallen 18.8 percent, ending today at 40-1/4, off 1-1/4, while Santa Fe shares have gained nine percent in the last year, finishing Tuesday at 15-1/4, up one.
Over the same period, the Philadelphia Stock Exchange gold and silver index fell 17 percent, while the Standard & Poor's 500 index grew 22 percent.

"Because Homestake's stock has underperformed for so long, they come to the party with shares that are less highly valued than most of the other senior-tier company, which gives them very weak currency to bid with," Lazarovici said.
"It is like going into the ring with Tyson," he said.
((--Brendan Intindola, Wall Street Desk, 212-859-1734)).
